title: Re: More on Anthropic's Scion ripping off Mononoke...
text: Re-designing a modern source control system for open source projects, you need to consider millions of developers have coding agents running on their computer and/or have Claude Code/Google/OpenAI coding agent accounts. And evidence from the Linux repo and many other GitHub repos, the open source projects are overflowing from coding agent submitted bug reports. If I was accepting a bug report and/or patch, I would want to know the stated problem and reasons why it's a problem, the desired state or fix and reasons why it's preferred, and if a patch is supplied, I would want verifiable proof of provenance: the signed session from the coding agent, including the prompts used to generate it paired with the changed code. This way open source maintenance can become truly decentralized.

title: Re: Opus 5.5 made our product launch video (linked)...
text:
We've been hacking on a side product and needed a launch video for it, but didn't want to pay an agency to make it. When Opus 5.5 came out and we saw some video examples, we tried to have it make us a video just from our codebase and some iterative feedback via Claude Code, and... it worked!!

It took a lot of iteration cycles over 2-3 days, and I found it helpful to spawn subagent review panels of various intelligence levels to provide feedback to another subagent pool of designer agents (kinda like a meta version of actor critic in RL). But overall massively cheaper (all on subscription plan token usage), and I didn't have to do any live product recording since it had the source code behind the site (RIP Screen Studio?)

Anyways, just wanted to share as more of us are making side projects, there's now a much easier to way to launch them to show them what they do.

If you made it this far and have any feedback on the video and site, drop it in the comments!
author: jackogrady

title: A misbehaving test MCP server for stress-testing your MCP client
text:
We needed an MCP server that misbehaves on our command to test our own MCP gateway at work, but could only find well-behaved MCPs. That’s why we built a misbehaving MCP server ourselves and now share it on here, might be helpful for others building MCP gateways.

It’s similar to the MCP Inspector, but lets you test your client not your server.

We called it MCP Test Kitchen and it’s a (also hosted) MCP server that lets you:

* Connect any client that takes a URL and an Authorization header (Cursor, Claude Desktop or your own). It answers both 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 clients and logs which protocol revision each request declared.

* Pick one of 6 scenarios: HTTP transport errors, JSON-RPC error responses, tool results flagged isError, elicitation, multi round-trip requests (MRTR) via a C# SDK v2 scenario, and a baseline with a configurable delay. JSON-RPC and tool errors can be set to fail on a specific call, so the first call succeeds and the second fails. Resources and prompts are always on, each with a deliberately broken variant. If you want other scenarios, let us know.

* Watch every request in a live log with timing, method, caller, status and protocol version.

* Clone a TypeScript reference client, pinned to the latest spec, with full source.

You can run it yourself, it’s open source. If you’d rather test it live, we also hosted it, but you need to login (Google or GitHub, needed for the token) and can get started immediately.

We’d appreciate feedback, that’s why we're posting. In the live tool, there is a box that emails us directly. We’re around to check feedback + other scenarios you wish it had.

* Link to the repo here: https://github.com/cakewalk-security/cakewalk-mcp-test-kitch...

* Live tool access here: https://mcp-test-kitchen.cakewalk.security/login

* More information on why we built this: https://www.cakewalk.security/mcp-test-kitchen/blog/wtf-simu...
author: george_ciobanu

title: Re: Neural networks are clean...
text:
Oof, right at the top it points to how people were apparently convinced of this situation from a single crappy example

You work in data science and you over indexed on a singular example to explain away an entire set of phenomenon??

My experience with more.... directly testable NN models that are small seems to be that they absolutely can be far too interconnected to make strong explanations. The structure and pathways they fall into don't have to make inherent sense to anything or anyone.

Is it possible that almost all nodes in a network being explainable with a singular feature that makes obvious sense to us is evidence of poor efficiency? The network hasn't been made to collapse learning or discover more effective organizational structures than what might make sense to us.

I don't think I have the fundamentals here to contribute though.

Working with some neural networks, you can somewhat feel the structure when you read between the lines of the output. You can sometimes feel that a threshold somewhere tripped and set the signals down an alternative path.

But confirmation bias and all that.

I hope interpretability has a breakthrough. It would make my job far easier and cooler.

I had figured the "Recursive generalization" was like, understood? Maybe I'm just too pop-sci brained. "Split categories into more on this new boundary" and "Combine two separate categories that aren't different enough" I thought were always the core verbs for working with bulk data. My mental model has never been formalized though, so is invalid.

I guess I never got a good sense of the examples they had which made it look like what was "obvious" or made sense to me wasn't always a good explanation in general. Neat.

It's interesting that meaningful examples both ways care about shapes so much, as your eyes encode edge finding and shapes really early in the signal path. It's why some optical illusions are so effective. It's awesome.

The whole "how do you test a neuron: Find a group of nouns and find where you can split them" is just how I find I think learning works. You build your mental model, and find the split points where it diverges from reality and you are wrong, and you refine. I feel like this is how I learned Random Forests conceptually, though surely that's not a valid comparison?

Apologies, not sure I have actually contributed anything here! I bet I misunderstood the entire article somehow. Specifically, I do not have the fundamentals of looking into visual models that he is really working from. But I always figured that when Data Scientists talk of "Features" in larger models, they explicitly meant these far more abstract representational "features". Doesn't the premise of model hijacking and abbliteration sort of presuppose that you have abstract "Reject" or "Safety" neuron paths? I've always understood this stuff as that neuron path, without weighting too much on individual neurons.

>I used to think of neurons as human-shaped nouns: one is a car, another is a curve.

I didn't think anyone was ever supposed to think this for human neurons! The way humans identify something as even a "Chair" is insanely abstract and cultural! Very specifically, the "building sub branches to disambiguate" is just, like, how you would expect a hierarchical human brain to self organize, right?

Some of this is why I've been so displeased with the interpretability research from Anthropic, where it felt like they just pointed new NNs at the disparate neurons of another NN and post hoc named them. I felt the paths were of importance at least but had no idea how to convey, interpret, or model that. Learn you a good math kids! Not having any formalisms hurts.

title: Re: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware...
text:
I reverse engineered almost all electronics I own. Does it have USB that does more than just charging? Connect it to a computer and let AI play with it. Unless it's heavily secured like a phone that's pretty much all you need to do. Making some old remote work with various devices? Simple. Dumping the entire state of Rodecaster and controlling it in any you want with software, or maybe a remote? Why not. Old printer no longer works with MacOS 27? Ask for new drivers and now it does.

The printer 'debugging' was one of the funniest and most WTF situations I've been in lately. I used Claude for the drivers and was essentially used by it as a meat sock to diagnose what's happening. Was the text on each line progressively less visible, ie did grayscale work? How about quality between page 1 and 2, the first one should be lower DPI. Ok now unload the paper so I can see the error and add some handling for it. Good, now load paper again we'll check the duplex.

If you are reasonably familiar with computers, it really is as simple as pointing a strong model at a device and burning some tokens. Feels like a fever dream, especially since I had very little idea about anything that has to do with hardware.

title: Show HN: Nexus – open-source local-first message routing for agents
text:
Hi HN, I built Nexus because I was tired of having multiple agents that I had to address one by one. I built an underlying mechanism where I could message all of them and have them have the capability to message each other and listen to wake events. I also got tired of having to run cron when I think that agents should have the capability to be event-driven.

Nexus is basically a daemon that runs and routes messages to where they need to be, it is fully customizable, which you can write scripts off of so that it will wake agents or route that message to an already existing agent. Right now it supports Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Hermes. But more are underway. It runs on your machine with no container required. (In my opinion, messaging within your machine should not require you to have to run a container.)

To try it:

  npm install --global @egregore/nexus
It runs on Linux, Windows and WSL today; It can run on mac but I havent fully tested it also you would have to build the binaries yourself for the latest version though. Full support for it is planned in the near future.
